source: Rosenbloom & Newell (1982) Learning by chunking: summary of a task and a model
finding: A production-system chunking model was run on the Seibel 1023-choice reaction task. Practice curves from the model are power-law in form, the same family as human curves. The authors argue the ubiquity of the power law points to one common mechanism, chunking.
numbers: Human data: Seibel task, 76,725 trials. Simulated practice curve: 72,633 trials. Chunk learned with fixed probability 0.01 per opportunity (assumed, not fitted to people). Performance measured in production-system cycles, not milliseconds.
quote: The ubiquity of the power law of practice argues for the presence of a single common underlying mechanism
limits: Model fit is by form (straight line on log-log), no goodness-of-fit statistic. Cycles are not time. The learning probability is a free assumption.
agent_relevance: Chunking predicts speedup that shrinks with each reuse. A stored-skill library should show diminishing returns per added skill; do not expect linear gains.

source: Rosenbloom & Newell (1982) Learning by chunking
finding: The full model was too costly to run for many trials. The long curve was produced by a meta-model that only simulates which chunks would be created, not by running the production system.
numbers: Full model run for a handful of trials only (nine successful trials for one hand are described). The 72,633-trial curve comes from the meta-model.
limits: The power-law result for long practice rests on a simplified simulation, not on the real learner. Early cost of chunking was already visible.
agent_relevance: Compiling experience into reusable units has real cost at learning time. Count that cost against the saving (guardrail G7).

source: Heathcote, Brown & Mewhort (2000) The power law repealed: the case for an exponential law of practice
finding: Refit of 40 data sets. Exponential beat power in every unaveraged set. Averaging across people biases the fit toward a power function. Search snippets only; paper text not opened.
numbers: 40 data sets, 7910 learning series, 475 subjects, 24 experiments (from repository abstract)
limits: Not opened. Rival APEX form fits better than power with an extra parameter.
agent_relevance: The Newell-Rosenbloom power law is the headline chunking prediction and it is contested. Do not build the agent on a power-law assumption about skill-library gains; measure the curve on our own data.

source: Evans, Brown, Mewhort & Heathcote (2018) Refining the law of practice, Psychological Review 125(4)
finding: Hierarchical Bayesian re-analysis that pools people without averaging. A delayed exponential law fit a clear majority of paradigms. The new form allows slow-fast-slow learning with power or exponential as limits. Snippets only.
numbers: Not read. Abstract says clear majority of paradigms favoured delayed exponential.
limits: Not opened. Full-text fetch returned 403.
agent_relevance: Plateaus, slumps and breakthroughs in learning are normal. A skill library may show a slow start before gains appear.

source: Rickard (1997) Bending the power law: a CMPL theory of strategy shifts and automatization, J Exp Psych General 126(3)
finding: On pseudo-arithmetic tasks the power law failed overall but held within each strategy (algorithm, then retrieval). Fits a component power laws account in which one strategy runs at a time. Challenges instance theory. Snippet only; the PDF would not open (certificate error, then damaged file).
numbers: Full shift to memory retrieval by about the 60th exposure per problem; learning highly specific to practiced problems (from abstract).
limits: Not opened. One task family.
agent_relevance: Learning is strategy-switching, not one smooth curve. Our schema should log which route (stored skill or fresh solve) answered each item; learning is specific to practiced problems.

source: Soar Manual, chapter 4 Procedural Knowledge Learning (chunking)
finding: A chunk is built when a substate creates a result in a superstate, at result creation not at impasse end. Chunks can compress hundreds of rule firings into one. Newer explanation-based chunking (EBBS, Soar 9.6) generalizes much more than older trace-based chunking. Procedural learning is off by default.
numbers: Arithmetic agent learned 1263 rules in Soar 9.4 and 8 general rules in 9.6.
limits: Manual statement of one lab's system, not a controlled study. Only the first 100,000 characters read.
agent_relevance: Over-specific storage is the default failure: 1263 vs 8 rules for the same competence. A stored skill should keep a variable-ized precondition, not the literal episode.

source: Soar Manual, chapter 4 (sources of over-general chunks)
finding: Documented sources of over-general chunks: search-control preferences that affect correctness are not tracked unless add-osk is on; probabilistic or random operator choice; negated conditions on substate-local data; quiescence-based tests; conflated working-memory elements from several rules; recalled memory treated as local. Over-general chunks are a known correctness risk, not just a speed risk.
numbers: No counts given. Local negations are allowed by default; a filter can reject such chunks.
quote: hundreds of rule firings can be compressed into a single rule firing
limits: Describes known cases, not their frequency.
agent_relevance: Map to our agent: a skill learned from a run that relied on a negative check, a random sample, or recalled memory may not be valid elsewhere. Store the preconditions it actually used and do not store results that came from sampling (G4).

source: Soar Manual, chapter 4 (when no chunk is built)
finding: Soar refuses to learn in some cases: a rule with no conditions, a result that depends on random or probabilistic selection, and a chunk that would refire on the elements that built it (chunk inhibition). Temporary justifications are deleted once their conditions stop matching.
numbers: None.
limits: Design rules from the architecture authors; no data on how often each fires.
agent_relevance: Gate on learning: do not store a skill from an unverified or sampled success. This matches guardrails G3 and G6 and our rule that a pass must be on something the answer was not fitted to.

source: Tambe, Newell & Rosenbloom (1990) The problem of expensive chunks and its solution by restricting expressiveness, Machine Learning 5:299-348
finding: Chunking cuts the number of subproblems and steps, but total run time can get much worse because some chunks are very costly to match. Authors show expensive chunks exist, explain causes, and restrict the representation language so each chunk is matched with bounded effort.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page; the full paper (pages 299-348) was not read.
limits: Only the abstract page was opened. Later work (Kim & Rosenbloom 1996) says the 1990 restriction does not give the bound in every case.
agent_relevance: Step count is the wrong metric. A big skill or memory library can cost more to search than it saves. Measure total tokens and latency including retrieval.

source: Kim & Rosenbloom (1996) Constraining learning with search control / learned-rule match cost (AAAI-96 paper 114)
finding: Learned rules built from a linear structure that ignores the original problem-solving structure can make the system slower than before learning. Making the learned rule's match follow the problem-solving structure (nonlinear) removes the slowdown. Utility problem shown with data in Grid tasks.
numbers: Grid task, 12 problems, average CPU seconds per problem: without learning 0.46; linear rule learning 1.42 (over 3 times slower); nonlinear rule learning 0.34.
limits: Two toy domains (Grid, Magic Square), one architecture. OCR text of the PDF was noisy; numbers read from tables.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for the utility problem: learning can make things slower by 3x. Same risk for retrieved skills or workflows that are put in context regardless of fit.

source: Kim & Rosenbloom (1996) AAAI-96 paper 114, Magic Square task
finding: In Magic Square, linear-rule learning could not even finish learning the first sub-problem: the learned rule reached over eight million partial matches and ran out of memory. Nonlinear learning was bounded by the no-learning time and was faster.
numbers: Over 8 million tokens for one learned rule. Without learning the time was greater than with nonlinear learning by a factor of nine (nine sub-problems).
limits: Single task, nine sub-problems, no variance reported.
agent_relevance: Worst case of an uncontrolled compiler is failure, not just no gain. Cap size of any stored skill and put a budget on retrieval.

source: Minton (1990) Quantitative results concerning the utility of explanation-based learning, Artificial Intelligence 42
finding: Origin of the utility problem: learned control rules can cost more to test than they save. PRODIGY/EBL keeps a rule only if average savings times frequency exceed match cost, using training data. Seen only through secondary summaries.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened; citation metadata differs between sources.
agent_relevance: Keep a stored skill only if measured saving times reuse rate beats its retrieval and context cost. This is a ready-made keep/drop rule.

source: Etzioni (1990) Why PRODIGY/EBL works, AAAI-90
finding: EBL speedup depends on whether the problem space allows non-recursive explanations. A static program transformer, STATIC, which does no learning from runs, matched PRODIGY/EBL in each of Minton's problem spaces.
numbers: STATIC matches PRODIGY/EBL in all of Minton's problem spaces (abstract only).
limits: Only the abstract page opened. Rival explanation: the gain came from the structure of the space, not from experience.
agent_relevance: Rival explanation worth testing: a skill library may help because it adds domain structure, not because it records experience. Control: give the agent hand-written skills vs self-induced ones (see SkillsBench b30).

source: Taatgen & Lee (2003) Production compilation: a simple mechanism to model complex skill acquisition, Human Factors 45(1):61-76
finding: ACT-R production compilation, with default parameters, predicted learning in a simulated air traffic control task. Fit was good overall and for the landing unit task, weaker for two other unit tasks, where the model was slower than people.
numbers: Human data: 65 undergraduates, 18 trials of 10 minutes (Ackerman 1988); model compared on trials 1-10. Planes landed: r2 = .97. Land unit task r2 = .98. Model slower on move and get-plane unit tasks. Model was run 5 times and averaged.
limits: One task, model starts with all declarative knowledge, so it beats people on trial 1. The authors choose the strategy by hand from task analysis.
agent_relevance: Compiled skill comes from first running a slow declarative route. Plan: first solve with explicit instructions, then compile the repeated pattern.

source: Taatgen & Lee (2003) Human Factors, background on Soar and ACT* learning
finding: Authors state Soar chunking sometimes produced procedures that were too general, and both Soar and ACT* produced ever larger macro-procedures that are hard to match. Anderson dropped ACT* knowledge compilation because of weak empirical support and 'computational misbehavior' (endless loops or early abort). Production compilation is claimed to avoid this by building only compact rules.
numbers: None; narrative claim.
limits: Claim is by rival-theory authors and is not tested head-to-head against chunking here.
agent_relevance: Two independent architectures hit the same wall (over-general and over-large compiled units). Favor many small compiled units over growing one large macro-skill.

source: Wang, Xie, Jiang et al. (2023) Voyager: an open-ended embodied agent with large language models
finding: Minecraft agent with a library of code skills. Without the skill library, early milestones are reached about as fast but the agent plateaus later. Diamond tool reached only by the full agent. Baselines without a library mostly fail the tech tree.
numbers: Tech tree, 3 trials, 160 iteration cap. Wooden: Voyager 6±2, no library 7±2, AutoGPT 92±72. Stone: 11±2, 9±4, 94±72. Iron: 21±7, 29±11, 135±103. Diamond: Voyager 102 (1 of 3), others 0 of 3. ReAct and Reflexion 0 of 3 at all levels. Headline: 63 unique items, 3.3x more than baselines.
limits: N=3 trials per condition. Figure 9 ablation values are only in a figure. GPT-4 only, which costs 15 times GPT-3.5.
agent_relevance: Library value shows late, on long horizons; early milestones barely differ (6 vs 7). Test our library on long chains, not first steps.

source: Voyager (2023) zero-shot generalization to a new world
finding: Transfer test in a fresh Minecraft world with unseen tasks, 50-iteration cap. Voyager with its library finished all four tasks in all trials and faster than Voyager without a library. Giving the library to AutoGPT helped only partly.
numbers: Iterations, 3 trials. Diamond pickaxe: Voyager 19±3 (3/3), without library 36 (2/3), AutoGPT with library 39 (1/3), AutoGPT 0/3. Golden sword: 18±7, 30±9, 30 (1/3). Lava bucket: 21±5, 27±9, 0/3. Compass: 18±2, 26±3, 30 (2/3).
limits: N=3, four tasks chosen by the authors. Difference between Voyager and Voyager-without-library is about 1.4x to 1.9x. The library's transfer partly depends on the Voyager prompting loop, since AutoGPT gets less from the same skills.
agent_relevance: Best measured transfer for a skill library: faster by about 40% on new tasks, and skills depend on the agent that uses them. A library alone is not the gain; it needs the loop that retrieves and checks it.

source: Voyager (2023) ablations and limits
finding: Largest ablation effects were not from the library: random curriculum cut discovered items 93 percent, removing self-verification cut them 73 percent. GPT-4 code gave 5.7 times more unique items than GPT-3.5. Authors admit the agent still gets stuck and writes wrong skills.
numbers: Random curriculum: -93 percent items. No self-verification: -73 percent. GPT-4 vs GPT-3.5: 5.7x.
quote: there are still cases where the agent gets stuck and fails to generate the correct skill
limits: Percentages read from text; no per-run variance in text. No independent replication found in search.
agent_relevance: Verification before storing a skill mattered more than the library itself. Matches our G2, G3, G6: store only checked successes.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried & Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory (ICML 2025)
finding: Agent induces reusable workflows from past tasks and puts them in memory. On WebArena (online, no labels, GPT-4) success rose from 23.5 percent to 35.5 percent. Beat human-written workflows (SteP, 33.0) and used fewer steps.
numbers: WebArena total success: AWM 35.5, BrowserGym baseline 23.5 (+12.0 points, +51.1 percent relative), SteP 33.0 (AWM +7.6 percent relative). Cross-template subset: AWM 33.2, SteP 32.1, BrowserGym 20.5. gpt-4-0613, temperature 0.
limits: Single run per cell, no confidence intervals reported. Success judged online by a model evaluator. Table 1 text was garbled in conversion; some per-site numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Strongest measured result for reusable procedural memory with a weak base model. Cross-template result (33.2 vs 20.5) shows it is not only template reuse.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory, Mind2Web
finding: Offline workflows from training data help in-domain; online workflows (induced from the agent's own test runs) generalize better as the train-test gap widens. Task-level success stays very low in absolute terms.
numbers: Step success, cross-task: MindAct 36.2 to AWM-offline 45.1 (+24.6 percent relative). Task success cross-task 2.0 to 4.8; cross-website 2.0 to 2.3 (offline) and 1.6 (online); cross-domain 1.0 to 0.7 (offline) and 1.7 (online). Cross-domain step success 18.6 to 32.6 (offline) and 35.5 (online).
limits: Task-level success under 5 percent everywhere, so the big step-level gains do not turn into solved tasks. Online induction can learn from wrong predictions.
agent_relevance: Step-level gains can hide no change in whole-task success. Our scoring must use whole-task checks.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory, workflow quality and combination
finding: Workflows induced offline and online do not add up: combining them scores between the two. Offline workflows seem to hurt online workflow quality. Induced workflows were used often but covered less than half of test steps.
numbers: Mind2Web cross-task task success: offline 4.8, online 4.0, both 1.6; step SR 45.1, 43.6, 44.5. Workflows per example 7.3 to 7.4. Utility rate 0.94 (WebArena), 0.91 (Mind2Web). Coverage 0.40 (Mind2Web). Function overlap 0.08 and 0.20.
limits: Small differences between conditions with no variance reported.
agent_relevance: More memory is not additive. Merging stored skill sets from different sources can lower results; keep one curated source and prune overlap.

source: Wang, Gandhi, Neubig & Fried (2025) Inducing programmatic skills for agentic tasks (ASI), COLM 2025
finding: Independent re-run of AWM with a stronger model (claude-3.5-sonnet) shows the memory gain is much smaller when the base agent is already stronger. Verified program skills added further gain and fewer steps.
numbers: WebArena success: GPT-4 vanilla 12.3 vs AWM 35.5 (in table). Claude vanilla 32.7, AWM 36.3 (+3.6 points), ASI 40.4. Steps: vanilla 5.6, AWM 5.9, ASI 5.0. ASI is +23.5 percent relative to vanilla and +11.3 percent relative to AWM.
limits: Same group as AWM, not fully independent. Comparison of the GPT vanilla (12.3) with the BrowserGym 23.5 in the AWM paper shows baselines vary by run setup.
agent_relevance: Gain from stored workflows fell from +12 points to +3.6 when the base model got stronger. Expect small gains for a strong model; test against the strong plain baseline (G7).

source: Wang et al. (2025) ASI, ablation of verification and format
finding: Checking a skill by running it before storing it raised success. Program-format skills placed only in memory worked worse than the same skills turned into text; as callable actions they worked best.
numbers: Shopping site success: unverified text 32.6; verified program (in memory) 36.4; verified text 39.0; verified program as actions 40.1. Only 15.6 percent of attempted program inductions passed verification, vs AWM adding a new skill 31.4 percent of the time.
limits: One website, small N. Authors note the agent tried to call skills not in its action space.
agent_relevance: Code-checked verification before storing added about 4 points. Execution check before compile fits G2/G3. Skills must match how they will be invoked.

source: Wang et al. (2025) ASI, scaled-up tasks, reuse and cross-website transfer
finding: On long compound tasks ASI beat both baselines with statistical support. In cross-website transfer, ASI beat vanilla significantly but not AWM on success. Reuse was frequent from few learned skills.
numbers: Scaled-up tasks t-tests: ASI vs AWM success t=-2.36, p=0.023; vs vanilla t=-4.09, p=0.0002. Cross-web: ASI vs AWM success p=0.167 (not significant), steps p=0.038; vs vanilla p=0.0007. Skills reused in 42.5 percent of cases; created from 7.6 percent of tasks. Shopping long tasks: vanilla success 41.7 vs AWM 68.3 vs ASI 100.0 (as printed, row alignment from text extraction is uncertain).
limits: Small task sets (tens per site), hand-built scaled-up tasks, same-lab baseline. Row alignment in the extracted table is uncertain.
agent_relevance: A few verified skills (7.6 percent of tasks) were reused on 42.5 percent of tasks: good evidence that compile-once pays when tasks repeat. Skill composition gains grow with task length.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) SkillWeaver: web agents can self-improve by discovering and honing skills
finding: Agent explores a site, writes API-like code skills, tests them, and reuses them. Gains on WebArena and live sites; skills written by a strong model also lift a weaker model. No gain on one site where steps need vision.
numbers: WebArena average success: GPT-4o 22.6 to 29.8 with skills (+32 percent relative); GPT-4o-mini 9.2 to 14.1. Online-Mind2Web average over 4 sites 40.2 to 56.2 (cars 11.1 to 11.1, flights 11.7 to 29.4). 160 exploration iterations per site; 57 live tasks. The paper text gives both 31.8 and 39.8 percent in places.
limits: Reported numbers disagree inside the paper (31.8 vs 32 vs 39.8). Only a part of the paper (first 100,000 characters) was read. Synthesized APIs were worse than human ones on GitLab and Maps. Failures: wrong skill chosen, wrong parameters.
agent_relevance: Skills cost 160 exploration steps per site up front. Failure modes are retrieval choice and argument errors, so add a precondition and argument check at call time.

source: Zhao et al. (2023) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners
finding: Agent extracts natural-language insights from success/failure pairs and retrieves past trajectories. Gains on all three tasks, with transfer between tasks. Insights matter more on reasoning, raw trajectories on embodied tasks.
numbers: HotpotQA success 28.0±1.4 (ReAct) to 39.0±1.7 (ExpeL). ALFWorld 40.0±0.3 to 59.0±0.3. WebShop reward 0.666 to 0.701. Ablation: HotpotQA insights-only 36, retrieve-only 31; ALFWorld insights-only 50, retrieve-only 55. Transfer HotpotQA to FEVER: ReAct 63, ExpeL transfer 70±0.7 (65±1.7 without task demos).
limits: Closed API models, text only. Training-set size curve only in a figure. Prompting only, no theory.
agent_relevance: Insight text (general rule) vs concrete trajectory (specific case) is the same trade as general vs specific chunks. Best measured cross-task transfer is +7 points (63 to 70).

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How memory management impacts LLM agents: an empirical study of experience-following behavior
finding: Adding every experience to memory made agents worse than a small fixed memory. Agents copy the past when a new task looks like a stored one, so errors spread. Adding only strictly checked experiences raised accuracy, and some deletion rules kept accuracy with far fewer entries.
numbers: Four agents, GPT-4o-mini. Success: fixed memory vs add-all vs strict: RegAgent 67.53 / 55.48 / 70.95; EHRAgent 16.75 / 13.05 / 38.50; AgentDriver 40.11 / 32.32 / 51.00; CIC-IoT 71.50 / 59.90 / 85.40. Add-all fell below fixed memory on every agent. Periodic deletion cut memory 65-80 percent; CIC-IoT lost 4.6 points. Input-output similarity correlation r about 1 on RegAgent.
limits: Paper contradicts itself on when strict addition passes the error-free case (about 2,000 or about 1,000 executions). Only the first 100,000 characters read. Evaluator quality drives results (coarse LLM judge much worse than strict).
agent_relevance: The LLM version of an over-general chunk. Store only checked successes; unfiltered memory lost 5 to 12 points vs a tiny fixed memory. Core support for guardrails G2, G3, G6.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank: scaling agent self-evolving with reasoning memory
finding: Memory of distilled strategies from the agent's own successes and failures beat no memory and beat two earlier memory methods on three benchmarks. Gains are small to moderate in points and smaller on Mind2Web.
numbers: WebArena success, no memory / Synapse / AWM / ReasoningBank: Gemini-2.5-flash 40.5 / 42.1 / 44.1 / 48.8; Gemini-2.5-pro 46.7 / 47.7 / 47.6 / 53.9; Claude-3.7 41.7 / 42.6 / 40.8 / 46.3. SWE-Bench-Verified: flash 34.2 to 38.8; pro 54.0 to 57.4. Mind2Web cross-task flash 3.3 to 4.8. Steps: 9.7 to 8.3 on WebArena.
limits: Single run per cell, no confidence intervals. LLM judge decides success of stored items. AWM is below no-memory for Claude-3.7 (40.8 vs 41.7). Authors' own method.
agent_relevance: On a strong base the best published memory gives +4.6 to +8.3 points. AWM sometimes fails to beat plain, so a library must be tested at equal tokens.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank, ablations
finding: Adding failure trajectories helped ReasoningBank and Synapse but hurt AWM, so the way memory is written decides whether failures are useful. Memory made extra sampling more useful: best-of-3 and parallel scaling gained with memory and barely without it.
numbers: WebArena-Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash, success-only vs with failures: Synapse 40.6 vs 41.7; AWM 44.4 vs 42.2; ReasoningBank 46.5 vs 49.7. Parallel scaling k=5: 55.1 with memory-aware scaling vs 52.4 plain; no-memory scaling only 39.0 to 42.2. k=1 baseline 49.7.
limits: One site, one backbone for ablations. Retrieval is simple embedding top-k.
agent_relevance: Failure lessons need their own format (what to avoid), not the same record as successes. Memory and sampling interact: do not assess them apart.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench: benchmarking how well agent skills work across diverse tasks
finding: Large benchmark of whether skills help. Human-curated skills raised pass rate by 16 points on average. Skills the model wrote for itself gave no benefit on average. Gains vary a lot by domain, and small curated skills sets beat large ones.
numbers: 84 tasks, 11 domains, 7 model-harness configs, 7,308 trajectories, 5 trials per task. Mean pass rate: no skills 24.3, curated 40.6 (+16.2). Self-generated -1.3 points on average (text), table shows 21.0. Domain: healthcare +51.9, manufacturing +41.9, software engineering +4.5. Haiku 4.5 with skills 27.7 vs Opus 4.5 without 22.0. 16 or 18 of 84 tasks got worse (versions differ).
limits: Skills add context, so gains may partly be extra text; authors say length-matched controls are needed. Terminal tasks only. Benchmark skills scored 10.1/12 on quality vs 6.2/12 in the wild. Version numbers (84/86 tasks, -1.3 vs 21.0) disagree inside the paper. Only the first 100,000 characters read.
agent_relevance: The most direct test of the chunking premise for LLMs: an agent writing its own skills got nothing. Value comes from checked, human-quality procedures. Skills must be built outside the model's own unchecked output.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench, skill size and form
finding: More skill text is not better. Four or more skills and comprehensive documentation lost most of the gain. Compact or detailed single skills worked best. Authors name two reasons self-written skills fail: vague procedures, and not noticing when specialist knowledge is needed.
numbers: Number of skills: 1 skill +17.8, 2-3 skills +18.6, 4+ skills +5.9 points. Complexity: detailed +18.8, compact +17.1, standard +10.1, comprehensive -2.9 points.
limits: Quote is the paper's example of a vague self-written skill. Confound: task type may vary with number of skills. Not randomized.
agent_relevance: Matches the Soar lesson on large macro-procedures (b15). Limit injected skills to 1 to 3 short ones per problem; select by code, not by the model (G5).

source: Laird, Rosenbloom & Newell (1986) Chunking in Soar: the anatomy of a general learning mechanism, Machine Learning 1:11-46
finding: Original chunking paper: macro-operator learning in Soar. Earlier papers reported improvement with practice, transfer and strategy acquisition on the Eight Puzzle and part of R1-Soar. Only abstracts and secondary summaries seen; full text not opened (DTIC copy gave 403).
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened. An informal summary page lists that Soar cannot recover from learning errors such as overgeneralization.
agent_relevance: The 'no recovery from over-general chunk' note motivates a delete-or-demote rule for stored skills that later fail (a track record per skill).
